# Temperature experiment

**PURPOSE:** Our interest lies in whether sex-baised temperature tolerance exists in 3 livebearing fishes due to dimorphism in size: sailfin mollies (*Poecilia latipinna*), Western mosquitofish (*Gambusia affinis*), and Panuco swordtails (*Xiphophorous nigrensis*). This stems from an observation of males dying when sampling during hot months but females surviving fine. 

**MAIN AIMS:**
  (1) compare female and male thermal tolerance across these three species of livebearing fishes (Family: Poeciliidae)
  (2) compare thermal tolerance across male morphs within a single livebearing species (*X. nigrensis*)

**HYPOTHESIS:** Preexisting sex differences in size affect resistance to environmental temperature change.


***
***
***

## Summery stats 

```{r}
#remove unnecessary columns
datTot <- rawTempData[,-c(4:6)]

#create long format df to easily summarize later
dat.long <- datTot %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(CTmax.C, CTmin.C),
    names_to = "Trial",
    values_to = "Value") %>%
  mutate(
    Trial = dplyr::recode(
      Trial,
      "CTmax.C" = "CTmax",
      "CTmin.C" = "CTmin"))

#gather summary stats
summ.stats <- dat.long %>%
  group_by(Species, Trial) %>%
  summarize(
    mean = mean(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd   = sd(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    min  = min(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    med  = median(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    max  = max(Value, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop")

#get n for each sex in each species
sex.df <- datTot %>%
  count(Species, Sex) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from  = Sex,
    values_from = n,
    values_fill = 0)

#final table
summ.stats.all <- summ.stats %>%
  left_join(sex.df, by = "Species") %>%
  mutate(
    mean_sd = sprintf("%.2f (%.2f)", mean, sd))

summ.stats.all

```


## Size stats

When separated by sex and species, we see that there appears to be an overlap between small swordtail males and swordtail females (although they differ from large swordtail males), overlap between males and females in sailfins, and very little overlap among males and females in mosquitofish. This is confirmed through wilcoxon/kruskal-wallis tests: sailfin males and females show no significant difference in length with a small effect size (although wide CI may indicate uncertainty in magnitude and direction of any small difference), male and female mosquitofish show a significant difference in size with a large effect size indicating females are almost always larger than males, and swordtail sex categories (female, large male, small male) show a significant difference in length (as expected since male classes are separated by size), with a significant pairwise comparison among all groups and a large effect size indicating small males < females < large males. 

Sexual dimorphism in length was evident for mosquitofish and among sex/morph groups in swordtails (although direction of size difference varied among morphs). Evidence for sexual dimorphism in our sailfin was inconclusive, with negligible effect sizes but a wide confidence interval.

Overall collinearity is low for CTmax and CTmin trials, but separation by species shows low collinearity of sex and size for sailfins in both trial types and high collinearity of sex and size for mosquitofish in both trial types (makes sense since males and females showed little overlap in size for mosquitofish). Collinearity is high for size and sex/morph class in swordtails, which again makes sense because male classes are determined by size. Will need to interpret model results with this in mind (can't really detect a sex-only difference after accounting for similar sizes in mosquitofish and swordtail because there are no similar sizes in swordtails).

**Length comparisons and effect size**

```{r}

#separate male classes in swordtails
size.data <- datTot %>%
  mutate(
    SizeGroup = case_when(
      Species == "Swordtail" & Sex == "female" ~ "Female",
      Species == "Swordtail" & Sex == "male" & Size.cat == "large" ~ "Large male",
      Species == "Swordtail" & Sex == "male" & Size.cat == "small" ~ "Small male",
      Species != "Swordtail" ~ as.character(Sex),
      TRUE ~ NA_character_))


#normality check by sex and species
normal <- size.data %>%
  group_by(Species, SizeGroup) %>%
summarize(statistic =shapiro.test(Size.mm)$statistic,
          p.value = shapiro.test(Size.mm)$p.value)

normal #all normal except female swordtail and male mosquitofish


#non-parametric test for size difference by species
size.test <- datTot %>%
  filter(Species != "Swordtail") %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarize(stat = wilcox.test(Size.mm ~ Sex)$statistic,
            p_value = wilcox.test(Size.mm~Sex)$p.value)

size.test #not significant for sailfin, but significant for mosquitofish

sw.size.test <- size.data %>%
  filter(Species == "Swordtail") %>%
  summarize(stat = kruskal.test(Size.mm ~ SizeGroup)$statistic,
            p_value = kruskal.test(Size.mm ~ SizeGroup)$p.value)

sw.size.test #significant difference among sex categories; makes sense since the male classes are determined by size

pw.dat <- size.data %>%
  filter(Species == "Swordtail")
pw.test <- pairwise.wilcox.test( pw.dat$Size.mm, pw.dat$SizeGroup, p.adjust.method = "BH")

pw.test #all pairs significantly different


#testing effect size
eff.size.tbl <- datTot %>%
  filter(Species != "Swordtail") %>%
  group_by(Species) %>%
  summarise({
    cd <- effsize::cliff.delta(Size.mm ~ Sex)
    tibble(
      delta= cd$estimate,
    CI_low = cd$conf.int[1],
    CI_high = cd$conf.int[2])})

eff.size.tbl #sailfins with small effect size (-0.16) but wide CI (-0.49, 0.23) so there is uncertainty in the magnitude and direction of sexual size dimorphism. mosquitofish on the other hand show a large effect size with females being larger than males (0.99, CI 0.92, 0.998).

comparison <- list(
  c("Female", "Small male"),
  c("Female", "Large male"),
  c("Small male", "Large male"))

sw.eff.size <- bind_rows(lapply(comparison, function (g) {
  x <- pw.dat$Size.mm[pw.dat$SizeGroup == g[1]]
  y <- pw.dat$Size.mm[pw.dat$SizeGroup == g[2]]
  cd <- effsize::cliff.delta(x,y)
  
  tibble(
    group1 = g[1],
    group2 = g[2],
    delta = unname(cd$estimate),
    CI_low = cd$conf.int[1],
    CI_high = cd$conf.int[2])  }))

sw.eff.size #large size effects for all three combos; size ranking as follows: small males -> females -> large males


```

**Collinearity** 

```{r}
library(lme4)
### CTmax ###
model1 <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species + Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)

vif(model1) #shows low levels of collinearity for all effects

vif.spp <- datTot %>%
  filter(Species != "Swordtail") %>% #since there are distinct size classes here
  group_by(Species) %>%
  group_modify( ~ {
    model <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = .x, REML = FALSE)
    v <- vif(model)
    
    tibble(
      Predictor = names(v),
      VIF = as.numeric(v), 
      Singular = isSingular(model)) }) %>%
  ungroup()

vif.spp #low collinearity for sailfins, but high for mosquitofish; makes sense since we saw large sexual size dimorphism in this species

vif.sw <- size.data %>%
  filter(Species == "Swordtail") %>% 
  group_modify( ~ {
    model <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ SizeGroup + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = .x, REML = FALSE)
    v <- vif(model)
    
    tibble::rownames_to_column(
      as.data.frame(v),
      var = "Predictor") %>%
      mutate(Singular = isSingular(model)) }) %>%
  ungroup()
vif.sw #adjusted GVIF for size group and size.mm indicate strong collinearity among size and sex/morph class; makese sense since the males are separated by size, but will need to keep this in mind when interpreting results. singular fit shows no variation in trial runs


### CTmin ###
model1 <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species + Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)

vif(model1) #shows low levels of collinearity for all effects

vif.spp <- datTot %>%

  group_modify( ~ {
    model <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = .x, REML = FALSE)
    v <- vif(model)
    
    tibble(
      Predictor = names(v),
      VIF = as.numeric(v), 
      Singular = isSingular(model)) }) %>%
  ungroup()

vif.spp #low collinearity for sailfins, but high for mosquitofish; makes sense since we saw large sexual size dimorphism in this species

vif.sw <- size.data %>%
  filter(Species == "Swordtail") %>% 
  group_modify( ~ {
    model <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ SizeGroup + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = .x, REML = FALSE)
    v <- vif(model)
    
    tibble::rownames_to_column(
      as.data.frame(v),
```

# **Analysis**

## **CTmax**

### Model Selection

Here, we will run linear mixed effects models with CTmax as our dependent variable, and sex, species, and size (plus their interaction) as our independent variables. We will select our final model based on ΔAIC scores from the 'MuMln' package.

**Results:** The model containing just species as a dependent variable was the most supported in our model selection (ΔAICc=0.0; weight=0.511). Adding size (mod1b) or sex (mod1c) or both (mod1d) did not improve fit, but as they are characters of interest will will still examine the coefficients for comparison.

```{r}
# All models
mod1 <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #does CTmax differ among spp?
mod1b <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #is body size associated with CTmax after accounting for species?
mod1c <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species + Sex + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #is sex associated with CTmax after accounting for species?
mod1d <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species + Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)       #are sex and size independently associated with CTmax? *Remember collinearity
mod1e <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species + Sex * Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)
      #does the relationship between size and CTmax differ between males and females?
mod1f <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species * Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)
      #do sex-associated differences in CTmax vary among species, after accounting for size?
mod1g <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Species *Size.mm + Sex + (1|file.id.max), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #does body size and CTmax vary among species after accounting for sex?

# Model selection
model.sel(mod1, mod1b, mod1c, mod1d, mod1e, mod1f, mod1g)

  ### Mod1 (species only effect) is the most supported model (ΔAICc=0; weight=0.511)
  ### Adding size (mod1b) or sex (mod1c) or both (mod1d) did not improve fit, but as they are characters of interest will will still examine the coefficients for comparison
  ### Interactive effects (mod1e-g) showed very weak support, so allowing sex or size to vary did not improve model fit enough to justify the additional parameters; also possible that it is unstable to add additional parameters given our low sample size

```

### Residual checks

Here, we will check if the model residuals are normal and homoscedastic using the 'DHARMa' package.

**Results:** All models showed no outlier deviation or heteroscedasticity. 

```{r}

# Species only model
simulationOutput <- simulateResiduals(mod1, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput, form = rawTempData$Species)

  ### All good!


# Species and size model
simulationOutput2 <- simulateResiduals(mod1b, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput2)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput2)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput2, form = rawTempData$Species)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput2, form = rawTempData$Size.mm)

  ### All good!

# Species and sex model
simulationOutput3 <- simulateResiduals(mod1c, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput3)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput3)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput3, form = rawTempData$Species)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput3, form = rawTempData$Sex)

  ### All good!

# Species and sex and size model
simulationOutput4 <- simulateResiduals(mod1d, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput4)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput4)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput4, form = rawTempData$Species)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput4, form = rawTempData$Sex)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput4, form = rawTempData$Size.mm)

  ### All good!


```


### Model Summary

We will determine the overall effect of species (anova from 'lmerTest' package; using Satterthwaite approximation due to small sample size of random effect), and calculate the estimated marginal means and a pairwise species comparison (emmeans package). Model summaries will provide us with the effect of sex and size on the model. 

**Results:** There is a significant effect of species for CTmax (P<0.001). Pairwise comparisons show swordtails to be significantly different to sailfin (p<0.001) and mosquitofish (p<0.001), but sailfin and mosquitofish do not significantly differ (p=0.061). Sex was confirmed as not a significant predictor in the model (estimate=0.284, SE=-.243, p=0.247).

```{r}
# SPECIES ONLY MODEL
 ## Overall species effect
anova(mod1, type = 2, ddf = "Satterthwaite") #significant (p<0.001)

 ## EMM & Pairwise comparisons

PW.sp.max <- emmeans(mod1, "Species", lmer.df = "satterthwaite")
summary(PW.sp.max) #EMM
pairs(PW.sp.max, adjust = "holm") #Pairwise results
      
 ## Plotting EMM

PW.df <- as.data.frame(confint(PW.sp.max))

ggplot(PW.df, aes(x=Species, y=emmean)) +
  geom_point(size=2) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=lower.CL, ymax=upper.CL), width=0.1) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 10)) +
  ylab("Predicted mean temperature (°C) \n") +
  xlab("\n Species") +
  theme_classic()

# SPECIES & SIZE MODEL

summary(mod1b)

# SPECIES & SEX MODEL

summary(mod1c)

# SPECIES, SIZE & SEX MODEL

summary(mod1d)

# SUMMARY TABLE
coef.table <- function(model, label, trait) {
  as.data.frame(coef(summary(model))) %>%
    rownames_to_column("Predictor") %>%
    filter(grepl(trait, Predictor)) %>%
    mutate(Model = label) %>%
    mutate(
      CI_low = Estimate - qt(0.975, df) * `Std. Error`,
      CI_high = Estimate + qt(0.975, df) * `Std. Error`) }

ctmax.results <- bind_rows(
  coef.table(mod1b, "B", "Size.mm"),
  coef.table(mod1c, "C", "^Sex"),
  coef.table(mod1d, "D", "Size.mm|^Sex"))
  
ctmax.results

```

## **CTmin**

### Model Selection

We will repeat the above analysis with CTmin as our dependent variable, and sex, species, and size (plus their interaction) as our independent variables. Then select our final model based on ΔAIC scores.

**Results:** The model containing species, sex, and size as dependent variables was the most supported in our model selection (ΔAICc=0.0; weight=0.267), but models containing just species + size (mod2b), species + sex (mod2c) or species only (mod2) had similar ΔAICc and weight values, meaning all 4 models are a competitive fit. 

```{r}
# All models
mod2 <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #does CTmin differ among spp?
mod2b <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #is body size associated with CTmin after accounting for species?
mod2c <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species + Sex + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE) 
      #is sex associated with CTmin after accounting for species?
mod2d <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species + Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)       #are sex and size independently associated with CTmin? *Remember collinearity
mod2e <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species + Sex * Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)
      #does the relationship between size and CTmin differ between males and females?
mod2f <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species * Sex + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)
      #do sex-associated differences in CTmin vary among species, after accounting for size?
mod2g <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Species *Size.mm + Sex + (1|file.id.min), data = datTot, REML = FALSE)
      #does body size and CTmin vary among species after accounting for sex?

# Model selection
model.sel(mod2, mod2b, mod2c, mod2d, mod2e, mod2f, mod2g)

  ### Mod2d (species + sex + size) is the most supported model (ΔAICc=0; weight=0.267), although mod2c (species + sex) and mod2b (species + size) are also well supported (mod2c: ΔAICc=018; weight=0.244; mod2b: ΔAICc=0.57; weight=0.201). Mod2 (species only) also shows moderate support (ΔAICc=1.31; weight=0.139).
  ### Interactive effects (mod1e-g) showed very weak support, so allowing sex or size to vary did not improve model fit enough to justify the additional parameters; also possible that it is unstable to add additional parameters given our low sample size

```

### Residual checks

Here, we will check if the model residuals are normal and homoscedastic.

**Results:** Both the species only (most supported) and species + sex model are heteroscedastic. This is driven by species-level differences in variation. Robust standard errors will allow us to assess the significance of the effects despite this heteroscedasticity. 

```{r}

# Species only model
simulationOutput <- simulateResiduals(mod2, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput, form = rawTempData$Species)

  ### All good!


# Species and size model
simulationOutput2 <- simulateResiduals(mod2b, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput2)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput2)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput2, form = rawTempData$Species)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput2, form = rawTempData$Size.mm)

  ### All good!

# Species and sex model
simulationOutput3 <- simulateResiduals(mod2c, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput3)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput3)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput3, form = rawTempData$Species)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput3, form = rawTempData$Sex)

  ### All good!

# Species and sex and size model
simulationOutput4 <- simulateResiduals(mod2d, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput4)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput4)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput4, form = rawTempData$Species)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput4, form = rawTempData$Sex)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput4, form = rawTempData$Size.mm)

  ### Quantitle deviation detected for lower quantile, but combined adjusted quantiles test ns
```


### Model Summary

Again, we will use robust standard errors to assess factor significance, as this method can tolerate the heteroscedasticity we detected in our model residuals. We will determine the overall effect of species, calculate the estimated marginal means and run a pairwise species comparison all using the robust variance-covariance matrix. Lastly, we will calculate robust standard errors to illustrate the effect of sex on the model. 

**Results:** There is a significant effect of species for CTmin (P<0.001). Pairwise comparisons show swordtails as significantly different from sailfin and mosquitofish, and the difference between sailfin and mosquitofish was marginal (0.050). Despite the additions of sex and size improving model fit, neither were statistically significant.

```{r}
# SPECIES ONLY MODEL
 ## Overall species effect
```

## **Across male morphs**

Males in the Panuco swordtail have three morphs determined by copy number at mc4r locus: large males (SL >= 32mm), intermediate males (26 < SL < 36), and small males (SL <= 25mm with defined gonopodium). The morphs have greater variation in size than the variation between large males and females. We compare thermal tolerance across male morphs (only large and small, no intermediate in our study) and females. 

### Models

For both CTmax and CTmin, a model of temperature ~ sex category was the most supported, although adding size was also competative for CTmax. 

```{r}
#swordtail only data frame; will use dat.plot df as it has male morphs already 
swordtail.df <- dat.plot %>%
  filter(Species == "Swordtail")


### CTmax ###
SWmod1 <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Sex.plot + (1|file.id.max), data = swordtail.df, REML = FALSE)
SWmod2 <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Sex.plot + Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = swordtail.df, REML = FALSE)
SWmod3 <- lmer(CTmax.C ~ Sex.plot * Size.mm + (1|file.id.max), data = swordtail.df, REML = FALSE)

model.sel(SWmod1, SWmod2, SWmod3)
    ### SWmod1 with best support (ΔAICc=0; weight=0.71) although adding size (SWmod2) is also competative (ΔAICc=1.86; weight=0.28). 

### CTmin ###
SWmod4 <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Sex.plot + (1|file.id.min), data = swordtail.df, REML = FALSE)
SWmod5 <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Sex.plot + Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = swordtail.df, REML = FALSE)
SWmod6 <- lmer(CTmin.C ~ Sex.plot * Size.mm + (1|file.id.min), data = swordtail.df, REML = FALSE)

model.sel(SWmod4, SWmod5, SWmod6)
    ### SWmod4 with best support (ΔAICc=0; weight=0.748); adding size or an interaction did not improve fit nor are competative models (ΔAICc >2).
```


### Residual checks

Here, we will check if the model residuals are normal and homoscedastic using the 'DHARMa' package.

**Results:** Residuals for all 3 models (SWmod1-mod3) pass.  

```{r}

# CTmax
simulationOutput <- simulateResiduals(SWmod1, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput, form = swordtail.df$Sex.plot)

  ### All good!


simulationOutput <- simulateResiduals(SWmod2, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput, form = swordtail.df$Sex.plot)

  ### All good!

# CTmin
simulationOutput <- simulateResiduals(SWmod4, n = 1000)

plot(simulationOutput)

plotResiduals(simulationOutput)
plotResiduals(simulationOutput, form = swordtail.df$Sex.plot) #threw a quantile deviation, but not sure if this is real or side effect of small samples
cat_test <- plotResiduals(simulationOutput, form = swordtail.df$Sex.plot)
cat_test$uniformity$p.value.cor # all = 1
cat_test$homogeneity #p = 0.836

  ### All good!

```

**Results:** Sex category (large male, small male, female) did not significantly affect thermal tolerance within swordtails across both temperature categories (CTmax: p=0.617; CTmin: p=0.275). This result is mirrored in all pairwise comparisons.

# **Power Analysis**

Based on the power of our current study, we will calculate the average temperature difference needed to detect a significant sex effect. 

**Results:** The actual temperature difference between males and females in each category was much lower than the simulated temperature differences needed to detect a sex effect given the power of our study (Actual: CTmax=0.2, CTmin=0.1; Simulated: CTmax=0.6, CTmin=0.3). While we found no statistically significant sex effect in any temperature category, smaller biologically meaningful differences can not be ruled out due to our limited sample size.

***NOTE:*** This will increase loading time; to reduce loading time, remove/comment out the following section and keep the comparisons table to view results.

Power simulation:

```{r}
# Function to simulate power and find minimum detectable sex difference
# Inputs:
#   nsim: number of simulations per effect size
#   species: vector of species names
#   nM, nF: vectors of males/females per species
#   sigma: residual SD from linear model
#   alpha: significance threshold
#   power_target: desired power (e.g., 0.8)
#   delta_range: vector of sex differences to test
#   trait_name: name of the trait (for labeling)

simulate_MDD <- function(nsim=1000, species, nM, nF, sigma, alpha=0.05,
                         power_target=0.8, delta_range=seq(0, 3, by=0.1),
                         trait_name="Trait") {
  
  power_results <- data.frame(delta = delta_range, power = NA)
  
  for(i in seq_along(delta_range)){
    sig_count <- 0
    for(j in 1:nsim){
      temp <- c()
      sex <- c()
      sp <- c()
      
      for(k in seq_along(species)){
        # simulate male and female data around delta/2 difference
        temp <- c(temp,
                  rnorm(nM[k], mean = delta_range[i]/2, sd = sigma),
                  rnorm(nF[k], mean = -delta_range[i]/2, sd = sigma))
        sex <- c(sex, rep(c("M","F"), times=c(nM[k], nF[k])))
        sp <- c(sp, rep(species[k], times=nM[k]+nF[k]))
      }
      
      df <- data.frame(temp=temp, sex=sex, species=sp)
      
      # Fit linear model
      m <- lm(temp ~ sex + species, data=df)
      
      # extract p-value for sex
      pval <- summary(m)$coefficients["sexM","Pr(>|t|)"]
      if(!is.na(pval) & pval < alpha) sig_count <- sig_count + 1
    }
    
    power_results$power[i] <- sig_count / nsim
  }
  
  # Find minimum detectable delta (closest to target power)
  closest <- power_results$delta[which.min(abs(power_results$power - power_target))]
  
  cat("\n---", trait_name, "---\n")
  cat("Minimum detectable sex difference for", power_target*100, "% power: ", closest, "\n\n")
  
  return(list(power_curve = power_results, MDD = closest))
} ### END FUNCTION

# ==========================

species <- c("sailfin","mosquitofish","swordtail")
nM <- c(20, 13, 15) #number of males for each species
nF <- c(20, 12, 15) #number of females for each species

# Sigma values are the residual SD from the above linear models
sigma_CTmax <- 0.9861918   # summary(mod1f)$sigma
sigma_CTmin <- 0.5801441   # summary(mod2f)$sigma

# Run simulations
MDD_CTmax <- simulate_MDD(species=species, nM=nM, nF=nF, sigma=sigma_CTmax, trait_name="CTmax") #0.6°C
MDD_CTmin <- simulate_MDD(species=species, nM=nM, nF=nF, sigma=sigma_CTmin, trait_name="CTmin") #0.3°C

CTmax_df <- MDD_CTmax$power_curve %>% mutate(Trait="CTmax", MDD=MDD_CTmax$MDD)
CTmin_df <- MDD_CTmin$power_curve %>% mutate(Trait="CTmin", MDD=MDD_CTmin$MDD)
power_all <- bind_rows(CTmax_df, CTmin_df)

# Plot
ggplot(power_all, aes(x=delta, y=power, color=Trait)) +
  geom_line(size=1.1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept=0.8, linetype="dashed", color="black") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept=MDD, color=Trait), linetype="dotted", size= 1) +
  labs(title="Power curves and minimum detectable sex differences",
       x="Sex difference (°C)",
       y="Power",
       color="Trait") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(text = element_text(size=12)) + 
  scale_color_manual(name="Trait",
                    values = c("CTmax"="#E1AF00", "CTmin"="#78B7C5"),
                    labels = c("CTmax"="CTmax", "CTmin"="CTmin"))



```

# **Summary**

We were interested in whether the sexual dimorphism found in many livebearing species played a role in thermal tolerance. We tested for sex-biased tolerance in CTmax and CTmin trials in three livebearing species: sailfin mollies (*P. latipinna*), Western mosquitofish (*G. affinis*), and Panuco swordtail (*X. nigrensis*). We also tested whether male morphs (i.e. large and small males) within one species (swordtail) affected thermal tolerance.

In both trials (CTmax, CTmin), sex and size did ***not*** influence thermal tolerance. Instead, only species differences affected thermal tolerance. In general, mosquitofish tolerated the most extreme temperatures, followed by sailfin. Swordtails had the narrowest and weakest thermal tolerance, owing likely to the consistency of temperature at their place of origin (e.g spring-fed rivers).

Likewise, male morphs did ***not*** influence thermal tolerance, further confirming that this is likely no detectable sex-biased thermal differences in our current setup. 

A power analysis shows that the actual detected sex differences in both categories is much lower than the simulated temperature differences needed in order to detect a sex-based effect given the power of our study. Therefore, smaller biologically meaningful differences can not be ruled out due to our limited sample size.
